name: Fermentation Lab
author: @praisejamesx
tagline: Track the batch, not just the bubble.
summary: A workspace for tracking a ferment with pH, temperature, visual cues, and your own array baseline — with food safety kept out of the smell channel.
whatItIs: A protocol, log, and decision-support workspace for home fermentation. It helps you record what changed, compare a batch to a reference blank on the same array, and stop when the primary controls say stop.
whatItIsNot: Not a pathogen test, not a pH meter, not a universal fermentation classifier, and not a cross-rig claim. A pleasant smell cannot clear a batch.

home.headline: The batch is the record, not the bubble.
home.detail: pH, temperature, recipe, and visible faults decide. The array only shows that something moved on this rig.
limits: A pleasant smell cannot clear a batch. pH, time, temperature, recipe, and visible evidence decide.
sources: FDA Bad Bug Book (2012); USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning (2015); 21 CFR 114.

widgets.headline: Food safety is not a smell test.
widgets.body: A Vial can tell you a sample changed on your array. It cannot tell you a batch is safe. pH, time, temperature, recipe, and visible evidence decide.
always: Use a calibrated pH meter and a tested recipe.
Log every batch: date, salt or brine, temperature, pH, and visual cues.
When in doubt, discard. Discard is a valid batch outcome.
never: Never use a pleasant smell to overrule mould, slime, or a pH above 4.6 in a low-acid ferment.
Never sell or serve a batch you cannot trace.
Never compare readings from a different array or rig.

widgets.title: What this workspace is allowed to claim

items.label: Array can do
items.hint: Same array, same sample prep, against your own reference blank.

items.label: Array cannot do
items.hint: No pathogen, toxin, or “safe to eat” call. Ever.

items.label: Primary controls
items.hint: These decide. The nose only flags that something changed.

widgets.title: The vessel, as a checklist
widgets.caption: Click a point. Every point is a place where a clean batch can turn into a risk.

hotspots.label: Airlock
hotspots.body: Gas should escape, not pressurise. Check the seal and keep the airlock clean. A dry airlock is not proof of safety.

hotspots.label: Lid / seal
hotspots.body: A sealed anaerobic vessel is exactly why low-acid ferments need a proven recipe and pH control. Do not improvise a low-acid anaerobic batch.

hotspots.label: Brine line
hotspots.body: Keep solids submerged. A surface exposed to air is a mould opportunity, not a flavour choice.

hotspots.label: Active ferment
hotspots.body: Bubbles and cloudiness are process cues. They are not a safety certificate. Log them with pH and temperature.

hotspots.label: Sensor port
hotspots.body: Use the array as a change detector against a clean reference on the same channels. Ethanol and acids can dominate the response; high VOC can saturate or poison MOX sensors.

steps.label: Prep
steps.body: Clean the vessel and hands. Weigh salt or measure brine. Label the batch. Record starting pH and temperature.

steps.label: Lag
steps.body: Bubbles may be quiet. Keep solids submerged. Log pH, temperature, smell, and anything visible.
steps.warn: No bubbles at day 3 is a prompt to verify pH and temperature, not to assume it is safe.

steps.label: Active
steps.body: Acidity should move toward the recipe target. Keep temperature stable. Off-odours, slime, or fuzzy growth are stop signals.

steps.label: Finish
steps.body: Chill or package exactly as the tested recipe says. Keep the batch record. Smell never overrides the recipe.

widgets.title: Batch log
widgets.description: The log is the valuable object. The sensor reading is one column, not the verdict.

widgets.title: pH trajectory
widgets.note: The line is your log. The example is not a target and not a safety curve. Follow the recipe and measure pH.

rules.when: pH above 4.6 after 48 h in a low-acid ferment
rules.then: Stop. Chill or discard per the recipe; verify with a calibrated meter. Do not rely on smell.

rules.when: Fuzzy, pink, black, or blue mould
rules.then: Discard. Do not salvage by removing the surface. Toxins can be invisible.

rules.when: Slime, rope, or a foul turn in the smell
No bubbles, no acidity, warm room, day 3
rules.then: Treat as stalled or risky. Verify pH and temperature; do not assume it is safe.

rules.when: Clean sour smell, pH in target, no visible faults
rules.then: Continue the protocol. This is not a safety certificate.

items.label: Vessel and hands clean
items.detail: No residue, no cracks, no exposed surfaces.

items.label: pH meter calibrated
items.detail: A reading you do not trust is worse than no reading.

items.label: Salt or brine measured by weight
items.detail: Volume spoons drift; weight is reproducible.

items.label: Temperature logged
items.detail: Warm is faster, not automatically safer.

items.label: Discard rule understood
items.detail: Decide now, not when the batch is emotionally valuable.

widgets.title: Use this with your rig
widgets.body: Record a clean reference blank, then a batch sample on the same channels and sample prep. Compare with Check. If the arrays differ, the app will refuse the comparison.

docs.title: How to use this workspace
body: Start one batch. Fill the batch fields, then add a reading whenever you measure pH, temperature, or inspect the vessel.
The array is a change detector: capture a clean reference and a sample on the same array, then compare them in Check. Do not compare a batch from one rig with a reference from another.
The stop rules are deliberately conservative. A sensor reading cannot clear a batch; it can only add a prompt to look, measure, or discard.

docs.title: What the sensor is actually doing
body: A MOX array responds to a mixture of volatile compounds. Ethanol, organic acids, and other fermentation products can dominate the response, and high concentrations can saturate or poison a sensor.
The useful signal is a change relative to a reference on the same array. The absolute number is not concentration and is not comparable across rigs.
Humidity, temperature, sample distance, and vessel headspace all change the reading. Log them as context, not as afterthoughts.

docs.title: What can go wrong
body: Low-acid, anaerobic ferments can support Clostridium botulinum growth. Smell is not a reliable botulinum test. Follow a tested recipe, use a calibrated pH meter, and respect the pH 4.6 boundary for low-acid foods.
Moulds can produce mycotoxins that are not removed by scraping the surface. Discard fuzzy or coloured growth.
Cross-contamination from hands, utensils, or an airlock turns a clean batch into an uncontrolled one.
A drifted or saturated sensor can make a changing batch look stable. The log and the primary measurements matter more than the trace.

docs.title: How to validate a Vial on your rig
body: Record a clean reference blank and at least three batch samples on the same array, with the same sample preparation and distance.
Use Check to compare the reference and the batch. Read the lower bound and the permutation p-value, not just the badge.
A sealed Vial is a claim about a closed-set comparison on the array that produced the evidence. It is not a transferable calibration and it is not a safety certification.

docs.title: Cleaning and traceability
body: Clean the vessel, lid, airlock, weights, and hands before the batch. Keep raw and finished batches separate.
Label every batch with date, recipe, salt or brine, and starting temperature. A batch you cannot trace is a batch you cannot debug.
